Self-driving laboratory for thin-film photovoltaics

Abstract
A self-driving laboratory autonomously synthesizes and characterizes thin-film perovskite solar cells. The system uses closed-loop optimization to maximize stability.

Introduction
Discovering stable perovskite photovoltaics demands navigating a complex multi-objective design space. Manual exploration is prohibitively slow.

Methods
The autonomous laboratory integrates a six-position spin-coater, an inert-atmosphere glovebox, an automated UV-Vis spectrometer, and an EQE stage. We use Bayesian optimization over compositional and processing variables. Closed-loop experimentation proceeds for 21 days without operator intervention; daylight saving time transitions are handled by the workflow orchestration layer.

Results
The closed-loop campaign discovers a perovskite composition with T90 lifetime exceeding 1100 hours under 1-sun illumination.

Figure 1. Schematic of the autonomous laboratory for perovskite photovoltaic discovery, showing the closed-loop integration of robotic synthesis and on-line characterization.

Figure 3. Discovered champion compositions and their stability metrics.

Discussion
The system demonstrates how closed-loop experimentation accelerates stability optimization for thin-film photovoltaics.
